title: the three controls that the wave C1 made dead move to the place it changed
intent: The wave repairs the proof of the package: the map said `unknown' and three claims stood **inconclusive**.  (1) **The reason.**  The wave C1 rewrote the three places that the registered controls of `wire-permission-request', `approvals-have-reply-kinds' and `always-is-remembered-for-the-session' mutate, so the `sed' of every control found nothing, the mutation changed nothing, and the check passed on an unchanged tree -- the class of F38, a guard that never fires.  Measured: on the commit `fe00b6b' (before the wave C1) the three patterns were there (1, 2 and 1 occurrences), on the tree of the wave they are 0, 0 and 0.  (2) **The repair.**  Only the control moves, to the place the wave C1 changed; the text, the falsifier, the scope, the requirements and the id of the three claims are the same, because the wave C1 changed no promise.  (3) **Every control was measured.**  The control of `wire-permission-request' turns the answer of the client into a refusal and the check refuses with `the allowed write did not run'; the control of `approvals-have-reply-kinds' stops the writing of the answer `always' into the rules and the check refuses with `the answer always was not written into the rules'; the control of `always-is-remembered-for-the-session' breaks the writing of the scope into the rule and the unit test refuses with `an always answer is remembered for the session'.  The honest tree is green over all three.  (4) **Two candidates were refused and the price is named.**  A mutation of the `always-p' of a nil scope changed nothing -- the code 0 -- so the control on it would have been vacuous; a mutation with a broken bracket gave the code 255, and a check that dies with 255 has not bitten.  (5) **The numbering is refined.**  The section 16.96 sent the findings F43 and F44 to the wave 105; the wave 105 carries the red line of the package (F54), and F43 and F44 wait for the wave 106, while F47, F48, F51 and F52 wait for the wave 107.
objection: The wave touches no kernel, and its price is named.  (a) **The proof of three claims was weaker than it looked**: the checks of the three claims were green and the controls of the three claims changed nothing, so the evidence of the three claims was not evidence at all; the wave says so and repairs it.  (b) **The control is a choice of the place**: a control that mutates a place the kernel does not promise is a control of an accident, and the place this wave chose is the place where the promise now lives -- the answer of the client becomes the decision, the writing of `always' into the rules, the writing of the scope into the rule.  (c) **A control that fires is not a control that measures**: the wave measured the three controls and refused two candidates, one of which changed nothing and one of which killed the check with the code 255; the control that is left refuses by the assertion of the claim, and the refusal names the subject.  (d) **The wave does not repair the falsifier of the wave 100**, which the same package breaks in the other direction: the check that proves the claim of the wave 101 reads the stat file of a process by itself, and the falsifier of the wave 100 is still literally broken by it.  That is the finding F43 and it waits for the wave 106.
note: The wave is the proof of the package, and every part of it was measured.  (1) **The three claims that stood inconclusive.**  `wire-permission-request', `approvals-have-reply-kinds' and `always-is-remembered-for-the-session' -- the map of the package said `unknown' after the gate, and the reason was not a flake: the controls mutated lines that the wave C1 had rewritten.  (2) **The places.**  `lib/yeah-acp.el' -- the branch that read `(equal option "allow-once")' became `(kind (list :effect :allow :reply kind))', because the answer of the client is now read through the canonical dictionary of the kinds; `lib/yeah-approval.el' -- the writing of the answer into the rules took the scope as an argument of its own; `lib/yeah-acp.el' -- the binding of the session id became a `let*' with two bindings.  (3) **The controls, after the move.**  `sed -i 's|(list :effect :allow :reply kind))|(list :effect :deny :reply kind))|' lib/yeah-acp.el'; `sed -i 's|(when (eq kind :always)|(when (eq kind :never)|' lib/yeah-approval.el'; `sed -i "/yeah-approval-remember-rule/,+3s/scoped)))/nil))/" lib/yeah-acp.el`.  (4) **The refusals, with their own words.**  `wire-perm: the allowed write did not run: "refused"'; `approvals: the answer always was not written into the rules' (and two more of the same check); `yeah-acp-an-always-answer-is-remembered-for-the-session' at `tests/unit/test-yeah-acp.el:292'.  (5) **The honest tree.**  The code 0 over the check of the wire permission, the check of the kinds of the answer and the unit test of the ACP.  (6) **The two refused candidates.**  The mutation of the `always-p' of a nil scope gave the code 0 -- it changed nothing, and a control on it would have been a comment; the mutation with a broken bracket gave the code 255 -- the check died instead of refusing (`ELISP_BEST_PRACTICES.md` section 11.5: `a check that dies with 255 has not bitten').  (7) **The live route.**  No live run was made for this wave: it touches no code of the kernel and only the evidence of the package.
